texts.facts: The petitioner is aggrieved with the alleged high handed action of the Health Inspectors in having closed down the bakery and manufacturing unit carried on by the petitioners, who are husband and wife. 2. The petitioners had, admittedly, two licenses; one for sale of bakery items, evidenced by Exhibit P3 [1st petitioner] and another for manufacturing of bakery items, evidenced by Exhibit P4 [2nd petitioner]. The petitioners submit that they had made some modifications and, hence, did not function the bakery for some time. However, the said contention is belied by the fact that the petitioners were functioning on 12.08.2016 when the Health Inspectors had inspected the property of the petitioners. It is also seen that the petitioners were carrying on the activities in an unhygienic manner. 3. A notice was issued, produced as Exhibit R8(b) by the Health Inspector. An intimation was also given to the Secretary, which is produced by the Secretary as Exhibit R1(a). Subsequent to that, the petitioners applied for a licence, as is seen from Exhibit R8(d) and R8(e). Admittedly the consideration was not made within the thirty days time as provided for in Section 236(3) of the Kerala Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 [for brevity "KPR Act"]. 4. The petitioners allege that on 21.10.2016, two Health Inspectors, along with the Secretary, President and Vice-President of the Panchayath came to the premises of the petitioners and closed down the unit. The Secretary and the Health Inspectors, impleaded as respondents 8 and 9, deny the same by separate counter affidavits. The Health Inspector submits that the locals made a Jayaram vs Secretary on 21 March, 2014 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/157144659/ 4 complaint to the Secretary and there was a commotion created in the premises by the locals; on information of which the Health Inspectors along with the President, Vice President and Secretary went to the premises and again warned the petitioners against the business being carried on without license and in an unhygienic manner. There was no closure effected, is the contention.
texts.arguments: 5. The petitioners, however, still submits that the premises were locked down by the President and Secretary who had also taken away the key. In the teeth of the assertion made by the Secretary and the Health Inspector that no locking of the premises were effected by them, this Court cannot direct the Secretary to open the premises. However, the petitioner would be entitled to break open the lock and enter the premises, especially since the Panchayat does not have a case of the premises having been locked down by them. The petitioners' Counsel then submits that there is a claim for damages for the injury caused to the petitioners by reason of the high handed action of the respondents. For that the purpose, the petitioners would have to avail of the appropriate civil remedies; especially since the officials of the Panchayath deny the incident totally and in that context an adjudication on facts is necessitated. 6. The next contention is with respect to the continuance of the business, which, the petitioners contend, can be carried on based on the deeming provision under sub-section (3) of section 236 of the KPR Act. Even according to the Panchayat, Exhibits R8(d) and R8(e) applications were filed on 16.08.2016. An inspection is said to have been conducted as per the endorsement in the said application, on 22.09.2016, which clearly proves that there was no consideration made within the thirty days. Hence, the petitioners are entitled to the deeming provision under sub-section (3) of Section 236. 7. The Health Inspector has a contention that since there is a delay in applying for renewal of the permit, there could be no benefit of the deeming provision granted to the petitioner. The said contention is raised, since the license admittedly expired on 31.03.2015 and an application for renewal was made on 16.08.2016. The issue was considered on the basis of the provisions in the Panchayat Raj (issue of Licence to Dangerous and Offensive Trades and Factories) Rules, 1996 (Kerala) by a learned Single Judge in Swapna Jestus K. v. Secretary, Pulpally Grama Panchayat and Another [2013 (1) KHC 450]. It was held that a conjoint reading of the Rules would show that the consequence of a delay in making an application would only be an additional fee. The Panchayat definitely would be entitled to insist for that additional fee or a penalty; but the renewal cannot be rejected nor can a demand be raised of the necessity for a fresh application for license. 8. The learned Government Pleader alertly points out that the petitioners' licence issued by Food Safety and Standards Authority has expired.
